== Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2747-2937

\subsection{Traits with comprises clauses read at the level of values}
\seclabel{revival-covering}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{internal-types};
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}; \secref{methods}; a draft note in the
subsection ``Export Statements'' of \secref{components}; the effect of
\secref{revival-comprises}.
\item[Change] \secref{internal-types} defines covering: a type covers another
when every value of the second is a value of the first; a type covers each of
its subtypes, and a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause is covered by the union
of its listed types; covering is not the subtype relation.
Its example concludes that $V$ covers $S \inter T$, where it concluded that
$V = S \inter T$, and a sentence says that a trait may stand between $S$ or $T$
and their listed types, so that $S \inter T$ is not in general equal to a named
type.
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} asks the argument types of the concrete
declarations to cover the argument type of the abstract declaration, where it
asked their union to equal it, and, in its example, for a definition for every
type listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause of \TYP{Molecule} or definitions that
together cover those types, where it asked for one for every immediate subtype.
Each of these four passages has a box.
The draft note says ``all its listed types'' where it said ``all its immediate
subtraits''; a draft note prints only in a draft build, so it has no box.
The effect of \secref{revival-comprises} no longer says that these passages are
not revised.
A correction of 9~October 2026 changes the last sentence of the box after the
example in \secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} and the sentence of this
entry's effect that repeats it.
They said that the compiled type checker checks that an object's concrete
methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, ``reading no \KWD{comprises}
clause''; they now say that it reads such clauses to do so, so that concrete
methods over the types that a trait lists together cover an abstract method
over that trait.
The normative text is unchanged.
An amendment of 14~October 2026 revises the sentence of \secref{methods} on
abstract methods: an object inheriting an abstract method defines it by a method
definition whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self parameter, is
that of the abstract method declaration, or by definitions whose parameter types
are subtypes of it and together cover it, or it is a static error, where the
sentence said only that the object must define a body expression for the method.
The sentence has a box.
The requirement of \secref{object-decls} that an object define all abstract
methods inherited from its supertraits is unchanged; the box says that it is
read in this sense.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that the passages that read a \KWD{comprises} clause at the
level of types are restated at the level of values, which is how
\secref{trait-decls} reads the clause since its revision of 28~September 2026
(\secref{revival-comprises}).
The team's later Types chapter names covering beside subtyping and exclusion as
a relation between types, and says that an instantiation of a trait with a
\KWD{comprises} clause ``is covered by the union'' of the listed types
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines 36--38
and 384--390, in the revival's repository).
Welterweight Fortress, the type group's calculus of 2012, reads the clause at
the level of values and counts an abstract declaration as covered when it is
implemented for all the types comprised
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick}, lines 21--22;
\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/fig-covered.tick}).
Under that reading a trait with static parameters may stand unlisted between a
trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types; an instantiation of it
is then a subtype of the closed trait and of no listed type, though every value
of it is a value of a listed type, so the passages' conclusions hold of values
and not of types.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
and \nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-judgement.md} in the
revival's repository.
The sentence that the correction of 9~October 2026 changes was false when it was
written: since 6~June 2012 the team's compiled type checker, testing whether an
abstract method's parameter type is a subtype of the union of the parameter
types of the concrete methods below it, tests whether the union of the types
that a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause lists is a subtype of that union
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala}
and \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala},
in the revival's repository).
It accepts an object whose methods over the two types that a trait lists cover
an abstract method over that trait, and refuses the same object when the trait
has no \KWD{comprises} clause.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-override/REPORT.md} in the
revival's repository.
The amendment of 14~October 2026 follows the revival's decision of 13~October
2026 that an object defines an inherited abstract method when its definitions
of that name at narrower parameter types together cover the abstract method's
parameter types, \KWD{comprises} clauses read as the compiled type checker
reads them; a definition at the abstract method's own parameter type is the
plain case.
It is the type group's rule of 2012.
The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, whether each
inherited abstract method ``is covered by one or more concrete definitions'',
its parameter type a subtype of the union of theirs (Steele, May 2012, in
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala},
in the revival's repository), and reads \KWD{comprises} clauses to do so since
6~June 2012.
Welterweight Fortress uses the same rules to check methods as functions, the
type of the trait or object within which the method is declared not considered
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/static.tick}, lines 27--47).
The sentence of \secref{methods} is older than that reading; the chapter's own
sentence on overloaded functional methods points to
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}, which asks for coverage, as the Meet Rule
does.
The team's library and tests define abstract methods by covering definitions:
the trait \TYP{RunRanges} of the component \TYP{Pairs}
(\nolinkurl{Library/Pairs.fss}) and the trait \TYP{dna} of the test
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/FileConversion.fss}, which the sentence read to
the letter would refuse.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/walk-load-readings-check.md}, section~2, in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] No example of this specification becomes invalid.
Covering is not subtyping: where an instantiation of a trait with static
parameters stands between $S$ and $T$ and their listed types, its value is a
value of $V$ but its static type is not a subtype of $V$, and the compiled type
checker refuses to assign it to a variable of type $V$; the interpreter, which
has no static types, runs such an assignment.
The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, that the
object's concrete methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, and reads
\KWD{comprises} clauses to do so: concrete methods over the types that a trait
lists together cover an abstract method over that trait; top-level abstract
function declarations run on neither implementation.
Since the amendment of 14~October 2026 the interpreter checks the same at load,
at each object without static parameters, reading \KWD{comprises} clauses as its
check of the Meet Rule reads them: it accepts an object whose definitions at
narrower parameter types together cover an inherited abstract method, as before,
and refuses one whose definitions do not cover it, where it accepted any one
definition at narrower parameter types before.
It does not check objects with static parameters and object expressions in
generic functions (row~665 of the revival's gap ledger), and it
refuses an object where its search through the \KWD{comprises} clauses
does not settle: a cycle, its bound of 10,000 steps or of 4,096 combinations of
parts, or a type it cannot read.
The compiled type checker splits a tuple of parameter types through
\KWD{comprises} clauses as the interpreter does, and refuses where its search
meets a cycle or passes the same bounds: it accepts an object whose concrete
methods cover an inherited abstract method of two parameters only through
combinations of the types that a trait lists, as the interpreter does.
It splits no tuple where the abstract method or a concrete method below it has
static parameters of its own, and so refuses an object whose concrete methods,
one of them with a static parameter of its own, cover such a method only
through those combinations (row~NEW-O-3 of the revival's gap ledger).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex},
lines 568--570:
\begin{quote}
because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
clause of $U$, any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$.  Thus,
$V = S \inter T$.
\end{quote}
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/functions.tex}, lines 377--378:

Furthermore, the union of the argument types of the concrete declarations for
\VAR{f} must be equal to \VAR{T}.
\end{quote}
and lines 413--415:

For the latter, the programmer must provide a definition for every immediate

\end{quote}
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/components/source-code.tex}, line
429, the words of the draft note's second item that changed:
\begin{quote}
provided that all its immediate subtraits are considered to have concrete
method declaration with that signature.
\end{quote}
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, lines 510--512:
\begin{quote}
An abstract method declaration declares an \emph{abstract method}; any object
inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the method.
\end{quote}
The effect of \secref{revival-comprises}, the revival's text of 28~September
2026, ended:
\begin{quote}
The passages that read a \KWD{comprises} clause at the level of types, the
intersection of two traits with such clauses (\secref{internal-types},
\secref{more-specific-rule}) and the definitions an abstract function
declaration requires (\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}), are not revised;
whether they are to be restated at the level of values is not settled.
\end{quote}
The box after the example in \secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}, the
revival's text of 30~September 2026, ended:
\begin{quote}
The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, that the
object's concrete methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, reading no

\end{quote}
and the effect of this entry said the same in its words.
\item[Route C] The same under route~C: the reading of a \KWD{comprises} clause
at the level of values does not depend on the rule on instantiations.

128	## 4. What the specification settles
129	
130	- **No Duplicates Rule.** It refuses two declarations each applicable to every call to which the other is (`overloading.tex:548-549`). A functional method's parameter type includes the self parameter's type at its position: functional methods "can be viewed as top-level function declarations" (`traits.tex`, "Method Declarations"). So both of row 707's pairs are refused, wherever self stands.
131	- **Coverage.** An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies at narrower parameter types that together cover it, comprises clauses read at the level of values (`traits.tex:627-648`, P-147, P-60). Row 709's bodies cover `(Side, Side)`. Row 708's one body covers only `(P1, P1, P1, P1, P1)`, so the object is refused however the search ends.
132	- **The bound.** The specification bounds no search. The bound of 4,096 combinations is the implementations' (decision 4).

- NEW-O-1 and NEW-O-2: a generic functional method beside a plain one in an object stops walk at load and stops the code generator.

F-145, F-223 and the skill's `references/interpreter.md:42` and `references/revival-changes.md:66` need their sentences on rows 707 to 709 rewritten.

## Revival change

**The change.**

1. **The No Duplicates Rule at two self positions.**
   - The team's checker: it counted two declarations as duplicates only where their parameter types were equivalent and their self parameters stood at one position (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:368` at `a874948ac`). So `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in one trait passed it, and the code generator stopped: "Likely bug in static analysis, apparently malformed overload set not rejected" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:409-411`).
   - The tree now: the checker refuses two functional methods with equivalent parameter types wherever their self parameters stand, "There are multiple declarations of f with the same parameter type", naming the domain of the declaration written first (`OverloadingChecker.scala:441-451`). Tests: `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositions`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsPlain`.
   - The reason: the No Duplicates Rule refuses two declarations each applicable to every call to which the other is (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:548-549`). The type group's paper of 2011 states "if $d_1 \ms d_2$ and $d_2 \ms d_1$ then $d_1 = d_2$" (`Papers/Types/rules.tick:158-161`). A functional method can be viewed as a top-level function (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Method Declarations"). The code generator's stop above is the measured failure.

2. **Coverage through comprises clauses in the checker.**
   - The team's checker (Steele, May 2012): it defined an inherited abstract method only where the method's parameter type was a subtype of the union of the covering definitions' parameter types (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala:103` at `a874948ac`). Its subtype relation splits one trait type through its comprises clause below a union, but compares a tuple with each member alone (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:159-166`). So definitions at `(Ping, Ping)`, `(Ping, Pong)` and `(Pong, Side)` under `g(self, x: Side, y: Side)`, with `Side comprises { Ping, Pong }`, were refused: "Domain (Side, Side) is not a subtype of OR((Ping, Pong),(Pong, Side),(Ping, Ping))".
   - The tree now: the checker splits each position of the parameter types through comprises clauses and asks that every combination of parts lie inside one definition's parameter types, within 10,000 steps and 4,096 combinations, as walk does (`AbstractMethodChecker.scala:124-181`). Test: `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/AbstractMethodCoveredPairs`. It does not split where a method has static parameters of its own (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXAbstractMethodCoveredPairsGeneric`).
   - The reason: the traits chapter defines the method by "definitions whose parameter types are subtypes of it and together cover it" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:627-648`). Welterweight Fortress's Covered rule counts an abstract declaration covered when it is implemented for all the types comprised (`Papers/Welterweight/fig-covered.tick`). The checker's refusal above is the measured failure.

3. **Walk refuses where its search for a cover does not settle.**
   - The team's walk: it counted any declaration with a body as defining an abstract method (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Constructor.java:404` at `a874948ac`). The revival's first coverage check accepted an object wherever its search did not settle.
   - The tree now: walk refuses there, at a cycle, a symbolic or unreadable type in the split, more than 10,000 steps or more than 4,096 combinations. It counts a definition whose parameter types it cannot read as no cover (`Constructor.java:462-518`). Test: `ProjectFortress/tests/AbstractMethodCoverUnsettledWalk.fss`.
   - The reason: the compiled checker refuses such an object: "Domain (D, D, D, D, D) is not a subtype of (P1, P1, P1, P1, P1)" (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXAbstractMethodCoverUnsettled`). Walk's own Meet Rule check refuses where its search does not settle (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:890`, `:894`). The measured failure: walk loaded that object and printed `1`.

**Provenance.** Each change and the decision it follows:
- Row 707: PLAN's line for row 707, listed under "Climb batch 14, listed for his review". It follows the No Duplicates Rule as climb batch 14's rung P restated it (row 696) and the type group's late word (P-26).
- Row 709: PLAN's line for row 709, under P-147 (item 51) and P-60.

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table was produced, 1 if it could not be. 20 s in the main tree,
# measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

# the earlier stages reported, so that nothing hides behind an early return; one table.
#
# Why it exists: Pavol's answer 11 (POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-26): the full measurement of the
# distance to the switch-over "becomes a report-only stage of phase 3's gates, whose job is
# driving it down". The checker-count stage beside it (../checker-count/run.sh) sees only
# the errors before each api's early return, 62 of about 1,740 on 2026-09-27.

# shadow sources and classes, the driver, the checker's caches (-Dfortress.caches) and the
# JVM's temporary directory (so Rats! leaves nothing in /tmp) go to the scratch directory
# (default: $TMPDIR or /tmp), and the caches are deleted at the end. It never removes
# /tmp/fortress*rats, which other runs on the machine use. Exit 0 if the table was

are each a subtype of the other, ``There are multiple declarations of \VAR{dup}

have static parameters and their parameter types mention one parameterized

other's parameter type is its bound (row~549).

declarations with the same number of parameters have static parameters with the
same bounds; it admits fewer overloadings than these chapters, so that its valid
programs are still valid, and its rules and its soundness claim are unchanged

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

component XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositions
export Executable

(* Two generic functional methods of one trait whose parameter types are each as specific as the other, self first in one and second in the other, break the No Duplicates Rule, a static error the type checker gives (overloading.tex, section "Declarations with Static Parameters"). *)

trait S
  f[\T extends S\](self, y: T): ZZ32 = 1
  f[\U extends S\](x: U, self): ZZ32 = 2
end
object O extends S end

run(): () = do
  println(f(O, O))
end

end
component AbstractMethodCoveredPairs
export Executable

(* An object defines an inherited abstract method of two parameters by bodies that cover it only through the combinations of the types a comprises clause lists, so the program compiles and runs (traits.tex, section "Method Declarations"). *)

trait Side comprises { Ping, Pong } end
object Ping extends Side end
object Pong extends Side end

trait Pairer
  g(self, x: Side, y: Side): ZZ32
end
object Joiner extends Pairer
  g(self, x: Ping, y: Ping): ZZ32 = 11
  g(self, x: Ping, y: Pong): ZZ32 = 12
  g(self, x: Pong, y: Side): ZZ32 = 13
end

run(): () = do
    assert(g(Joiner, Ping, Ping), 11, "g over Ping and Ping")
    assert(g(Joiner, Ping, Pong), 12, "g over Ping and Pong")
    assert(g(Joiner, Pong, Ping), 13, "g over Pong and Ping")
    assert(g(Joiner, Pong, Pong), 13, "g over Pong and Pong")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

\section{Declarations with Static Parameters}
\seclabel{overloading-static-params}

The rules above compare the parameter types and the return types of
declarations without static parameters.
A declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose parameter
type ranges over every instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their
bounds (\secref{overloading-terms}).
A declaration $d_1$ is more specific than a declaration $d_2$ when $d_2$ is
applicable to every call to which $d_1$ is applicable, and not the other way
round (\secref{resolving-overloading}); where neither has static parameters,
this is the relation $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$ of the rules above.
A set of overloaded declarations, some or all of which have static parameters,
is a valid overloading when every pair $d_1$, $d_2$ of them satisfies the
following three rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each applicable to every
call to which the other is applicable.
\item
The \emph{Meet Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ exclude each other, or one of them is more
specific than the other, or some declaration of the set is more specific than
both and applicable to every call to which both are applicable.
\item
The \emph{Return Type Rule}: if $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$, then for
every argument type other than \TYP{BottomType} to which $d_1$ is applicable,
and for every instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to it, some instance of $d_1$
is applicable to it whose return type is a subtype of the return type of that
instance of $d_2$.
\end{itemize}
